answer_text:
Great question! Here's a detailed breakdown of why we turn pale or greenish when we're sick:

---

## 🩸 Why We Turn Pale When Sick

The primary cause of looking pale when sick comes down to **blood flow and vasoconstriction** (the narrowing of blood vessels).

Vasoconstriction is the narrowing of the blood vessels resulting from contraction of the muscular wall of the vessels, in particular the large arteries and small arterioles. When blood vessels constrict, the flow of blood is restricted or decreased — and this makes the skin turn paler because less blood reaches the surface.

Our skin gets its rosy, pinkish color from oxygenated blood flowing near the surface. The degree of pallor or ruddiness is mainly a function of the amount of blood in the skin — with little blood in the venous plexus, the skin appears pale.

---

## 🤢 The Role of Nausea

When we feel nauseated, the body triggers a chain of physiological responses. The green-ness of being sick is typically associated with nausea. When we get nauseous, it's probably because there's not a lot of blood going to our heads — resulting in that dizzy feeling.

Usually the body redirects blood to an affected area of illness, which lowers effective blood pressure and results in a person appearing pale. Often when you are sick, you become a little dehydrated, which can do the same thing.

Additionally, a physical or psychological event can prompt an immediate sympathetic response that causes cutaneous vasoconstriction. Such vasoconstriction can make a patient's skin feel "clammy" — moist, cool, and usually pale — as a sympathetic response to stress, where stress causes the release of hormones such as epinephrine and norepinephrine.

---

## 🟢 Why "Green"?

People don't literally turn bright green, but there's a subtle shift in skin tone that our brains are wired to detect. Within one hour of the activation of an innate immune response, clear changes in skin coloration occur — facial skin becomes lighter and less red. This loss of red tones can give the face a subtly greenish or sallow appearance by comparison.

The human brain is super sensitive to how faces change color — which is probably why, despite "going green in the face" being more subtle than, say, blushing red, we still agree on it as a common experience. We are also exceptional at detecting whether or not people are feeling sick based on their faces. This makes sense, since being around sick people gets you sick — the best way to avoid getting sick is to avoid sick people.

---

## 🤧 Bonus: The Green Snot Connection

Part of the cultural association of "green" with sickness also has to do with snot. When we're noticeably sick and blow our noses, our snot is a lot thicker and greener — owing largely to an enzyme called myeloperoxidase, which is used by neutrophils (a type of white blood cell) to kill bacteria.

---

## In Summary

| Cause | Effect on Appearance |
|---|---|
| Vasoconstriction (blood vessels narrowing) | Skin turns pale/white |
| Blood redirected away from skin | Less rosy color, more sallow |
| Loss of red tones | Skin appears subtly greenish |
| Dehydration | Enhances pallor |
| Sympathetic nervous system stress response | Clammy, pale, cold skin |

So the "pale and green" look is really your body's emergency response system at work — diverting resources away from your skin and toward the organs that need it most!
